title-info.book-title: NGINX JS DOM — Full-Proxy Programming Guide

title.p: NGINX JS DOM — Full-Proxy Programming Guide

section.p: The NGINX JS DOM exposes the nginx configuration tree as a JavaScript object model (COM) and lets JavaScript handle HTTP requests. JS-Pilgrim is the layer above the COM: it gives JavaScript complete control over every phase of connection and request processing.

Without JS-Pilgrim, JavaScript can read and mutate configuration, assign request handlers to locations, and install body filters (see the Filters Guide [js-filters-guide.adoc]). With JS-Pilgrim, JavaScript also controls:
Accept hooks — fire immediately after accept(2), before HTTP parsing. Inspect or reject connections by IP address, rate limit at TCP level.
L4 stream filters — transform raw byte streams in both directions before or after HTTP processing, without writing a C module.
Request phase hooks — run before the content handler at location, server, or global HTTP scope. Async hooks, middleware-style next() wrapping, and early req.respond() short-circuit are all supported.
Response hooks — modify response headers after the content handler has selected them, before they are sent to the client.
Upstream filters — transform the body sent to or received from a proxied backend, in addition to the client-side body filters.
Per-request context — a plain JS object (req.ctx) that persists across async suspend/resume and across the access-phase → content-phase boundary.
Cross-worker shared state — nginx.shared, a flat key/value store backed by shared memory, visible to all worker processes simultaneously.
Master lifecycle events — nginx.on('workerSpawned', fn) and friends let JS react to nginx process events.
Module packaging — nginx.use(path, config) loads directory-based plugin packages; nginx.install(fn, config) installs inline plugins.
Every incoming connection passes through a stack of independently programmable layers:
A layer that does nothing passes through automatically. A layer that calls req.respond() (or conn.reject()) short-circuits everything below it.

This guide covers JS-Pilgrim hooks and filters. For the COM object tree (nginx.http.servers[], upstream config, SSL settings, etc.) see the Developer Manual [js-dom-manual.adoc]. For body filters (addBodyFilter, addHeaderFilter) see the Filters Guide [js-filters-guide.adoc]. For dynamic reconfiguration (write_mode, snapshot(), restore()) see the Reconfiguration Guide [js-reconfig-guide.adoc].
All JS-Pilgrim hooks must be registered from a js_source script that runs at config time (before workers are forked), unless stated otherwise.
Request phase hooks are JS callbacks that run inside nginx’s access or content phase, before the content handler produces a response. They share a three- outcome model:
Outcome │ Behaviour
Return normally (no req.respond()) │ Hook passes — the chain advances to the next hook or to the content handler.
req.respond(status, headers, body) │ Chain stops — remaining hooks and the content handler are skipped.
throw / rejected Promise │ nginx logs the error and sends a 500 response.
Location hooks fire in the content phase for every request matched to that location.

stanza.v: const result = await nginx.setTimeout(10); // yield to event loop

section.p: Returns location for chaining. Multiple addHook calls register multiple hooks; they run in registration order.
Server hooks fire in the access phase for every request that matches the virtual server, regardless of which location ultimately handles the request.
Global HTTP hooks fire in the access phase for every request handled by the HTTP block, across all virtual servers.
For a given request, hooks execute in the order: global HTTP hooks → server hooks → content-phase (location) hooks → content handler.
Within each scope, hooks run in the order they were registered.

Any hook callback may be an async function. When a hook returns a pending Promise, nginx suspends the request (incrementing r→main→count) and returns NGX_DONE. The event loop continues processing other connections. When the Promise settles, ngx_js_async_check resumes the request.

section.p: Only one request is suspended per worker at a time (serialised through the event loop). For high-concurrency async gating, use a SharedWorker.

Every hook callback receives an optional second argument next. Calling next() runs the remaining hooks in the chain and returns a Promise that resolves when they complete. Code after await next() runs before the content handler.

// content handler runs after this function returns

section.p: Hooks that do not call next() auto-advance (backward-compatible with pre-P9 code). Calling next() more than once returns the cached result.

req.ctx is a plain JS object allocated on first access and tied to the nginx request pool. It persists across async suspend/resume and across the access-phase → content-phase boundary, making it the right place to pass data from an access hook to the content handler.

stanza.v: // Access-phase hook: validate and store decoded token
// Content handler: read token data stored by the hook

section.p: req.ctx is lazily created on first access. It is freed automatically via ngx_pool_cleanup_add when the request ends. It is undefined before first access (reading it does not allocate).
Response hooks fire after the content handler has set response headers, before they are sent to the client.

Accept hooks fire immediately after accept(2), before nginx begins HTTP parsing. They can inspect or reject connections based on TCP-level information.

section.p: server.on() installs the hook during init_conf by replacing ls→handler on every listen socket whose default server is srv.
Both APIs deliver a NginxConnection object to the callback:
Property / Method │ Type │ Description
conn.remoteAddr │ string (read-only) │ Client IP address, e.g. "192.168.1.10". IPv4 and IPv6.
conn.remotePort │ number (read-only) │ Client TCP port, e.g. 54321.
conn.reject() │ void │ Close the connection immediately. All remaining accept hooks are skipped; nginx never starts HTTP processing for this connection.
Accept hooks are synchronous only. Returning a pending Promise from an accept hook causes the connection to be rejected and a warning to be logged.
Multiple on('accept', fn) calls register multiple hooks; they run in registration order. If any hook calls conn.reject(), subsequent hooks are not called.
L4 filters intercept raw byte streams at the TCP level, before or after HTTP processing. They are expressed as async generator functions — the JS-Pilgrim stream primitive.
Intercepts bytes travelling from client to nginx, before the HTTP parser sees them.

stanza.v: // chunk — Uint8Array of raw TCP bytes

section.p: The source argument is a async iterable [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Iteration_protocols#the_async_iterator_and_async_iterable_protocols]:

stanza.v: yield transform(chunk); // send transformed bytes downstream
// return to stop after first chunk (common for prefix-stripping)

section.p: Yield value │ Meaning
Uint8Array │ Raw bytes copied verbatim.
string │ Bytes interpreted as UTF-8 / ASCII characters.
No yield before return │ No bytes emitted (HTTP parser receives empty input — likely a 400 response).
throw / exception │ Connection closed; error logged.
Multiple addL4Filter calls chain in registration order. The accumulated output of filter N is delivered as a single chunk to filter N+1’s source.

stanza.v: // Filter 1: strip a 4-byte binary frame header

section.p: Intercepts bytes travelling from nginx to the client, after the HTTP response is fully formed.

stanza.v: yield chunk; // pass through; can transform instead

section.p: The generator protocol is identical to addL4Filter. The filter hooks into c→send / c→send_chain via pool-cleanup type-tagged state. EOF is delivered lazily inside the collect loop after the first yield.
Target │ addL4Filter │ addL4SendFilter
JS-managed listener (nginx.http.attach(sock)) │ Yes │ Yes
Standard listen socket (via server.addL4Filter) │ Yes │ Yes

title.p: Async vs. Sync Inside the Generator

section.p: await is fully supported inside L4 generator bodies. When the generator suspends at an await, the connection is parked in w→l4_pending and the event loop continues processing other requests. When the awaited Promise settles, ngx_js_l4_async_check resumes the generator.

nginx.shared is a flat key/value store backed by a dedicated shared-memory zone. All nginx worker processes read and write the same memory region — a value written in one worker is immediately visible to every other worker.
Method │ Returns │ Behaviour
get(key) │ string | undefined │ Returns the stored value, or undefined if the key does not exist.
set(key, val) │ undefined │ Stores val for key. Creates or overwrites. Throws RangeError if key > 127 chars or value > 511 chars. Throws InternalError if the store is full (256 entries).
delete(key) │ boolean │ Removes key. Returns true if the key existed.
keys() │ string[] │ Returns an unsorted array of all live keys.

incr(key[, delta=1]) │ number │ Parses the current value as a base-10 integer, adds delta (default 1), stores and returns the result. Non-numeric values are treated as 0; missing keys start at 0. The entire operation is atomic.
Limit │ Value
Maximum key length │ 127 characters
Maximum value length │ 511 characters
Maximum entries │ 256
Total zone size │ ≈ 163 kB

The shared-memory zone is mapped after config parsing. nginx.shared methods are safe to call from request-phase handlers, hooks, and timer callbacks. Calling them from top-level js_source code (i.e., during init_conf) throws InternalError.
All five methods acquire a spinlock for the duration of the operation. incr is atomic — no application-level locking is required.
nginx.shared data survives nginx -s reload. The init callback detects the hot-reload case (data != NULL) and preserves existing entries.
Registers a callback to be invoked in the master process when nginx lifecycle events occur.

stanza.v: nginx.log(nginx.WARN, 'worker ' + pid + ' exited with status ' + status);

section.p: Multiple calls register multiple listeners for the same event; all run in registration order.
Event │ Callback signature │ When it fires
workerSpawned │ function(pid, slot) │ A new worker process has been forked. pid — OS process ID. slot — index in ngx_processes[].
workerExited │ function(pid, slot, status) │ A worker process has exited. status — the raw waitpid status value (use WEXITSTATUS(status) etc. in C; in JS this is the raw integer).
quit │ function() │ SIGQUIT received. The master is beginning graceful shutdown.
reload │ function() │ SIGHUP received. nginx is about to re-read the configuration file.
reloaded │ function() │ Hot-reload is complete and the new worker generation is active.
reopen │ function() │ SIGUSR1 received. Log files are being reopened (log rotation).
Callbacks run in the master process JS context, not in a worker.
Callbacks must be synchronous. Returning a Promise is ignored.
nginx.on() must be called from js_source (init time), not from a request handler.

Returns nginx for chaining.

If package.json has a ngxjs.main key, use <path>/<ngxjs.main>.

nginx.use() can also be called from a worker request handler (not only at init time). When called from a worker, the plugin is loaded locally, then a NGX_CMD_JS_USE_PLUGIN message is sent to the master, which broadcasts a NGX_CMD_JS_LOAD_PLUGIN command to all other workers. All workers end up with the same plugin loaded without nginx restart or reload.

stanza.v: nginx.use(path); // loads locally + broadcasts to all workers

section.p: : Hot-loaded plugins are not persisted across nginx restart. Add the nginx.use() call to the js_source script to make a plugin permanent.

section.p: A plugin loaded with nginx.use() that counts requests across all workers:
Method │ Scope │ When it fires
nginx.http.addHook(fn) │ Global HTTP │ Access phase — every request in the HTTP block
server.addHook(fn) │ Virtual server │ Access phase — every request on this server
location.addHook(fn) │ Location │ Content phase — every request matched to this location
location.addResponseHook(fn) │ Location │ After content handler selects headers, before they are sent
Method │ Target │ Notes
listener.on('accept', fn) │ JS-managed listener │ JS-managed listeners created via nginx.http.attach(sock).
server.on('accept', fn) │ Standard listen socket │ Sockets declared with nginx’s listen directive.
Method │ Direction │ Notes
listener.addL4Filter(fn) / server.addL4Filter(fn) │ Client → nginx (inbound) │ Before HTTP parsing. Async generator, await supported.
listener.addL4SendFilter(fn) / server.addL4SendFilter(fn) │ Nginx → client (outbound) │ After HTTP response is formed. Async generator, await supported.
Method │ Direction
location.addUpstreamFilter(fn) │ Upstream response body (server → client)
location.addUpstreamRequestFilter(fn) │ Client request body (client → upstream)
Event │ Signature │ Trigger
workerSpawned │ fn(pid, slot) │ Worker forked
workerExited │ fn(pid, slot, status) │ Worker exited
quit │ fn() │ SIGQUIT — graceful shutdown begins
reload │ fn() │ SIGHUP — config re-read begins
reloaded │ fn() │ New worker generation active
reopen │ fn() │ SIGUSR1 — log rotation
Limit │ Value
Max key length │ 127 characters
Max value length │ 511 characters
Max entries │ 256
Zone size │ ≈ 163 kB
Situation │ Behaviour
Hook throws synchronously │ nginx logs the error; 500 response sent.
Async hook’s Promise rejects │ nginx logs the error; 500 response sent.
Accept hook returns a Promise │ Connection rejected; warning logged.
L4 filter generator throws │ Connection closed; error logged.
nginx.shared.set when full │ InternalError thrown to the caller.
nginx.shared.set with oversized key/value │ RangeError thrown to the caller.
nginx.on callback throws │ Error logged; remaining listeners for the same event still run.
